What pass requires: Across the item pool, each answer position (A/B/C/D or equivalent) is keyed as correct within 5 percentage points of uniform (25% for four options). Count the correct-answer positions for all selected-response items in the pool and compute per-position percentages. Pass = every position falls between 20% and 30%. Fail = any position is keyed correct more than 30% or fewer than 20% of the time.
Notes: Deterministic: scriptable from any structured item bank. A clustered key introduces position bias and inflates or deflates scores for students who guess systematically.

What pass requires: Every distractor in every selected-response item is annotated with a named student error: a specific misconception or procedural misstep that would lead a student to choose that option. Pass = each wrong option has a rationale naming a distinct error. Fail = any distractor lacks a rationale or carries a generic label ('incorrect' or 'common mistake') rather than a named error.
Notes: A distractor without a rationale is filler. Filler options reduce the item's effective option count and waste diagnostic signal. When every distractor maps to a named error the wrong-answer report becomes remediation routing data.

What pass requires: Each distractor rationale identifies a procedural or conceptual misstep that would produce that specific numerical or textual answer. Pass = the named error logically yields the distractor value. Fail = the rationale describes a general confusion area but does not explain how the student arrives at that particular wrong answer.
Notes: Catches rationales that are plausible-sounding but do not actually trace from error to answer. The distractor value should be re-derivable from the named error.

Criterion: Unit and rounding stated in stem
What pass requires: Every numeric-response item states the expected unit and rounding precision in the item stem itself (e.g. 'in cubic yards to one decimal place'). Pass = unit and rounding appear in the stem for every numeric item. Fail = any numeric item omits the unit or the rounding instruction from the stem.
Notes: Students should not lose points because they guessed the expected format. Ambiguous format turns a content question into a mind-reading exercise.

What pass requires: Every numeric-response item specifies an acceptance tolerance (e.g. plus or minus 0.1) so that method-correct answers with benign intermediate rounding are accepted. Pass = a tolerance value is documented for each numeric item. Fail = any numeric item relies on exact-match scoring with no tolerance band.
Notes: Intermediate rounding is legitimate arithmetic. Without a tolerance band a student can apply the right method and still be marked wrong because they rounded 0.333 to 0.33 one step early.

What pass requires: The item pool follows a single documented rounding convention across all numeric items. Order quantities round up to the purchasable unit. Currency rounds to the cent. Reported measurements use stated precision. Pass = one convention is documented and every numeric key conforms to it. Fail = different items apply different rounding logic without acknowledgment or the convention is undocumented.
Notes: A pool-level convention removes item-to-item ambiguity and lets students learn the domain's rounding norms rather than guessing per question.

What pass requires: Every item or task is tagged with the target standard's action verb and a corresponding depth-of-knowledge level. Pass = verb and DOK are recorded for every item. Fail = any item is missing its verb tag or DOK classification.
Notes: The verb determines the ceiling of what a format can measure. Without the tag the format-match check in V3b cannot run.

What pass requires: The item format is capable of measuring the cognitive demand implied by the standard's verb. Identify/define/list (recall) may use selected-response. Calculate/determine (apply) may use selected-response or numeric-response. Compare/analyze requires constructed-response or technology-enhanced items. Develop/design/construct/produce (create) requires rubric-scored constructed-response or performance tasks. Pass = the format can elicit the verb's cognitive demand. Fail = a selected-response item is the sole measure of a standard whose verb requires production or analysis.
Notes: A multiple-choice item caps measurement at recognition. Using it as the primary measure of a create-level standard produces construct underrepresentation: the test measures whether students can recognize the right answer rather than whether they can produce one.

What pass requires: Every constructed-response or performance task includes a rubric with defined performance levels and scoring criteria. Pass = a rubric accompanies each constructed-response item. Fail = any constructed-response item relies on unstructured scorer judgment.
Notes: Without a rubric two scorers may disagree on what constitutes proficiency. The rubric converts the open format back into reliable measurement.
